name: Intrepid’s top half
intro: This is where the top half of Intrepid hit the Moon on 20 November 1969. After carrying Pete Conrad and Alan Bean back to their command module, the empty cabin was steered into the ground to make the first moonquake ever made on purpose. Its crater has never been confirmed. The see-through cabin hanging here shows how Intrepid’s top half looked before it hit.

hotspots.title: Somewhere here
hotspots.text: Intrepid’s cabin struck at 1.68 km per second, about 70 km from the landing site. Nobody has confirmed its crater yet, so this spot is a best guess from 1969 tracking.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: Coming in sideways
hotspots.text: It hit at a very shallow angle, so it probably smeared along the ground and broke apart instead of digging one neat round crater.

source.label: NSSDCA: Apollo impact sites on the Moon

hotspots.title: The empty cabin
hotspots.text: This was the crew’s cabin. It had no seats: the astronauts flew it standing up. Once Conrad and Bean had moved into the command module, the cabin was cut loose.

photo.alt: A small spacecraft with legs flies high above a cratered grey landscape.
photo.caption: Intrepid in orbit on 19 November 1969, before landing; the top half came back up alone the next day.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item as12-51-7507 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The first moonquake
hotspots.text: The seismometer the crew had left behind recorded the crash. The Moon kept vibrating for nearly an hour, a huge surprise, showing that its broken-up outer rock carries shaking very well.

source.label: NASA SP-235: Apollo 12 Preliminary Science Report

photo.alt: Wavy lines drawn on a long strip of paper.
photo.caption: The seismometer recording of the crash, printed out at Mission Control on 20 November 1969.
photo.licenseEvidence: NASA Image and Video Library item S69-59547 (JSC); no third-party credit or copyright notice on the item. NASA: images and video "generally are not subject to copyright in the United States" (https://www.nasa.gov/nasa-brand-center/images-and-media/).

hotspots.title: The ride home
hotspots.text: Under the cabin sat one small rocket engine with about 15,000 newtons of push. It had no throttle, only on and off, and it had to work the first time to lift the crew off the Moon.

hotspots.title: Only the top half
hotspots.text: This is just the top half of the lander: about 2.8 meters tall and a little over 4 meters wide. The bottom half served as its launch pad and is still standing at the landing site.

funFact: It came in almost sideways, only about 3.7 degrees above the horizon, like a stone skimming across a pond.
whyLeft: It had finished its only job, getting the crew back to orbit, so mission control used it one last time as a hammer to test the new seismometer.
repurpose: Nothing is left to reuse except scattered metal. Finding the pieces would show how a spacecraft shatters when it hits the Moon at high speed.

source.label: Estimate; a possible gouge with dark streaks spotted in LROC images (Stooke 2017), not confirmed
